name: Cytocare

card.summary: A range of injectable skin boosters that combine non-crosslinked hyaluronic acid with vitamins, amino acids and other ingredients, used to hydrate and refresh the skin.
card.note: Injected skin products carry infection and injection-site risks and should be given by a qualified practitioner.

quick.overview:
Cytocare is a brand of injectable skin boosters made by the French company Revitacare. The products are sold to clinics and combine non-crosslinked hyaluronic acid with a blend of vitamins, amino acids, minerals and other ingredients, aimed at the face, neck and decolletage.

The aim is smoother, more hydrated and fresher-looking skin rather than added volume. This approach belongs to the wider family of mesotherapy and skin-booster treatments, whose cosmetic effects have been little studied in standard clinical trials, and no peer-reviewed trials of Cytocare itself appear in the literature cited here.
quick.how: Practitioners place very small injections into the skin in a grid pattern, often as a short series of sessions spaced weeks apart. Different versions in the range carry different hyaluronic acid amounts (seller listings name them 502, 516, 532, 640 and 715). Skin-booster sessions are typically combined with a skincare routine and sun protection.
quick.risks: Typical risks of skin injections are redness, swelling, bruising, lumps and infection. Wikipedia's mesotherapy article reports clinic outbreaks of skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection linked to unhygienic practice. Products and injections should be handled by licensed professionals and availability depends on the country.

lead: Cytocare is the name of a range of injectable skin-revitalising products from Revitacare, a French company. Product listings describe them as non-crosslinked hyaluronic acid combined with a complex of amino acids, vitamins, minerals and other ingredients, delivered into the dermis by microinjection for the face, neck and decolletage. The range is organised by hyaluronic acid content, with names such as 502, 516, 532, 640 and 715. These descriptions come from seller and clinic listings and are promotional, not clinical evidence.

Users in appearance circles discuss skin boosters as a way to improve hydration, smoothness and glow without adding volume the way fillers do. The idea is that hyaluronic acid binds water and the added nutrients support the skin, which the manufacturer describes as supporting cellular regeneration and collagen production.

Mesotherapy, the broader technique, is described by Wikipedia as injecting vitamins, plant extracts, hormones and hyaluronic acid into the skin to hydrate and nourish it, with cosmetic uses not tested in standard clinical trials but with case studies, and with a small 10-patient study of facial multivitamin mesotherapy finding no clinically relevant rejuvenation benefit [1].

chain: Microinjections of hyaluronic acid and nutrients into the dermis
Skin holds more water and feels hydrated
angle.text: The intended effect is better skin texture and hydration, particularly on the face, neck and chest. Providers and manufacturers describe it as a skin-quality treatment rather than a contouring one.

infobox: Non-crosslinked hyaluronic acid with amino acids, vitamins and minerals (per seller listings)

paras: Seller and clinic pages describe Cytocare as a skin-rejuvenating solution built on non-crosslinked hyaluronic acid together with a multi-ingredient complex of amino acids, vitamins, minerals, nucleic acids, a coenzyme and an antioxidant. Exact ingredient counts differ between listings. The range is sorted by hyaluronic acid content from the lowest 502 to the highest 715 and is injected into the dermis.

Cytocare sits within mesotherapy, which uses intradermal injection of vitamins, plant extracts and hyaluronic acid to hydrate and nourish the skin [1]. Wikipedia notes its cosmetic uses have not been tested in standard clinical trials and describes critics, including a dermatologic surgeon, who say supporting data are lacking [1]. Practitioners and manufacturers, by contrast, describe skin boosters as a way to improve hydration and skin quality.

Wikipedia reports that clients at an Australian clinic developed skin abscesses and one had a mycobacterial infection, and that France briefly banned mesotherapy for fat removal in 2011 before lifting the ban after investigators traced problems to unhygienic conditions [1]. The US FDA does not regulate what practitioners inject; state medical boards do [1].
No studies found. Studies of the wider category are small; Wikipedia cites a 10-patient study of facial multivitamin mesotherapy that found no clinically relevant rejuvenation benefit [1].
